You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Battery health often evolves from an initial regime of slow capacity decay to a fast decay regime, due to catastrophic electrochemical reactions to cause the battery failure. The signals of such failure, however, often emerge much earlier during cycling, an early detection of which may help prevent the failure through real-time adjustment of cycling procedures. Here we demonstrate the integration of machine learning module directly into electrochemical battery test stations to constantly detect the signals from battery current and voltage profiles, followed by reinforcement learning–based real-time adjustment of cycling procedures for greatly elongated battery lifetime. We use solid-state lithium metal batteries to demonstrate this proof-of-concept implementation of built-in intelligence for future battery management systems, leveraging their high current density and fast cycling to generate abundant data and greatly shorten the development feedback loop. This intelligent approach improves battery lifetime by 265% and accumulative specific energy based on active material by 250% at 80% state of health, which is achieved through an effective control of detrimental interface reactions. This work showcases a pathway toward real-time artificial intelligence control of batteries for longevity and safety beyond human expertise.

---

## Introduction

The Li-ion battery is one of the most powerful technologies in our era for decarbonization and combating climate change 1–4. The longevity and safety concerns, however, constantly challenge its applications since the birth of the technology. One typical failure mode in Li-ion battery is the lithium dendrite induced short circuits or side reactions. The development of solid-state batteries shows that Li dendrite penetration may be prevented through hierarchical structure and interface designs of the negative electrode and electrolyte layers 5–8. However, Li dendrite can still cause various problems in solid-state batteries through its high reactivity with electrolyte and negative electrode materials 9–13, where fast capacity decay upon cycling can often be observed. For example, in Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2a, these solid-state batteries tested in our lab used relatively low negative to positive electrode capacity ratios (N/P ratio), which is preferred for practical batteries but is also a factor that can often boost Li dendrite growth or interface reaction, and hence battery failure. The capacity retention of these batteries is nonlinear, often with a “kneepoint” 14–16, beyond which rapid decline in capacity occurs. The origin of the kneepoint is complicated and lacks unified explanations 17,18. In Li-ion battery, it can often be caused by Li dendrite penetration induced internal short circuit, while in our solid-state batteries it is more likely related to the Li dendrite growth induced interface reactions. When the kneepoint appears in the battery cycling, both state of health (SOH) and remaining useful life (RUL) will drop quickly. SOH and RUL are two performance metrics widely used in the battery industry to describe the status of batteries. Previous modeling and artificial intelligence (AI) based methods also focused on the two metrics in their predictions 19–23. Nevertheless, the emergence of the kneepoint always challenges the prediction due to the dramatic change of capacity decay rate across the point 14,24.

For a given battery configuration, it was noticed that charging strategy can influence the lifetime 25,26. Derived from the primitive constant current (CC) and constant voltage (CV), the various fast charging strategies nowadays are mainly categorized into multi-stage CC-CV or pulse current based on charging waveform 27,28 and optimization control based on battery models 29,30. However, online modulation of charging strategies with battery cycling based on the real-time status of a running battery has not been implemented, as it requires real-time diagnosis of batteries and the decision-making capability of the program. In most previous cases, a charging strategy was firstly optimized and then the fixed strategy was executed to every cycle throughout the cycling test.

In this work, we develop a platform, as depicted in Fig. 1a, where the machine learning intelligence, consisting of two key modules of state perception and intelligent cycling, is connected with a running battery through the battery test station. The tester operates as both the experimental instrument and the physical main body for real-time integration of the AI agent running on the workstation. The platform can thus monitor the current battery state and then based on the detected data in previous N cycles decide how to change the battery cycling procedures for any following N cycles, where N is chosen to be 3 and the cycling procedures include various C-rates (1C = 150 mA/g) and voltage cutoffs in this particular work. As shown in the detailed workflow (Fig. 1b), the AI workstation directly communicates with the tester hardware via physical connection of COM APIs over TCP/IP. Every 3-cycle data is employed to evaluate the battery state and adaptively control the charging strategy. This implementation supports real-time closed-loop control without relying on proprietary vendor software.

As a proof-of-concept demonstration, we utilize the fast charging and discharging capability of our solid-state batteries to 20C-rate at low positive electrode loading 5, to greatly accelerate the data generation and reduce the feedback time in the proof-of-concept development. This enabled rapid lifetime cycling and efficient model iteration. While commercial Li-ion batteries offer better reproducibility, their limited rate capability would substantially prolong the experimental timeline, especially under AI-extended lifetimes. However, implementing our approach to commercial Li-ion battery and BMS system will be an obvious next step through the collaboration with the battery industry. Nonetheless, our strategy in principle could also be adapted to conventional Li-ion batteries or systems.

---

## Results

Our results highlight the built-in intelligence for fast charging capability of solid-state lithium metal batteries, where both longevity and SOH stability of batteries are greatly improved. In comparison with the control batteries with conventional fixed strategies, our real-time AI for battery charging strategy significantly postponed or even prevented the occurrence of the kneepoint before the industrial standard of 80% SOH. It is worth noting that neither the authors, the research field as far as we know, nor our AI platform has any a priori knowledge of a clear microscopic failure mechanism related to the kneepoint of these batteries. Interestingly, however, our experimental characterization and computational modeling later show that AI did identify an optimal strategy within our framework to modulate the evolution of the most relevant interface reaction, with the mechanism being discussed. This suggests the potential of such AI platform to help achieve fundamental understandings in battery electrochemistry as well.

More specifically, the state perception module detects battery states evolution with cycling in three different states of stable, transitional, and decay ones (Fig. 2a). While 0.8 SOH is commonly used in industrial settings as the end-of-life (EOL) threshold, the definition of state segmentation is to isolate and examine the rapid degradation behavior around the knee point. The transitional state represents a temporary yet critical period where internal failures and side reactions accelerate and have not yet stabilized. That means a battery in the transitional state, especially in an early stage of the state, can possibly return to the stable state through intelligent cycling (e.g., Fig. 2d, e). Only after the fast degradation phase does the battery enter the final decay state, characterized by a slower rate of capacity loss at very low capacities. The transitional state contains the kneepoint, with the two boundaries decided by first and second derivatives in a capacity retention profile. The left boundary of the transitional state is defined as when the acceleration, or second derivative, becomes continuously negative, and the right boundary is when velocity, or the first derivative, reaches its minimum negative value. The state definition here is supported by our experimental characterization and reflects the evolution of dominant electrochemical reactions in the batteries.

These solid-state batteries follow a configuration of NMC811 as positive electrode, multilayer electrolytes as separator, and Li/Graphite as negative electrode, i.e., Li/Graphite|LPSCl|LGPS|LPSCl|NMC811, where NMC811 represents LiNi0.82Mn0.07Co0.11O2, LPSCl represents Li5.5PS4.5Cl1.5 and LGPS represents Li10GeP2S12. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) cross-section images of the batteries at different cycling stages in Fig. 2b show the evolution of reactions at the LGPS|LPSCl interface. In the stable state, the interface remains overall intact, with only isolated dark spots occasionally observed, suggesting that the local area is with low Z number in chemical elements based on the contrast mechanism of the backscattered electron microscopy. As the battery progresses into the transitional state with cycling, more black points stay close to each other at the interface and eventually connect into a black line region in the decay state. Deep into the decay state, the interface region becomes thicker with voids but less dark 31,32. Energy dispersive X-Ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping further shows that the dark regions is rich in O and Ge, deficient in P and S (Supplementary Fig. 2), indicating the evolution is dominated by interface reactions between Li metal dendrite and LGPS electrolyte, with Li-Ge-rich local decomposition products initially generated at the transitional state and more elements of S and Cl later enter the reaction region deep into the decay state. Note although Li cannot be directly detected by EDS, it can react with oxygen thus trap them locally to mark the location of Li.

A historical dataset in the research group of such Li||NMC811 solid-state batteries with the knee point feature in the capacity retention test (Supplementary Fig. 1) was further used to train the neural network in order to predict the state of a running battery from the voltage and current data (Methods). Notably, this dataset is very scalable as it is generated by diverse solid-state batteries by various group members for different projects previously, rather than coming from a dedicated collection for this particular project. That said, the consistent positive electrode/negative electrode configuration ensures a focused evaluation of the ability of our model to generalize across different degradation patterns induced by electrolyte variations. To construct the training samples, each battery is not treated as the data unit; instead, the model ingests abundant 3-cycle segmental data from the entire cycling of each cell as the data unit.

The state perception module can read the running battery on the voltage and current data of every 3 cycles. Since the geometrical shape details in voltage profiles as an ensemble reflect the collective behavior of the internal electrochemical reactions, the state perception module, equivalently speaking, monitor these reactions in situ for a working battery, providing sufficient nonlinearity and complexity for the input layer of deep neural network (DNN) models. The real-time state information of the past 3 cycles each time is then fed into the intelligent cycling module to evaluate how to change the charging strategies for the next 3 cycles. We employ reinforcement learning (RL) to provide dynamic decision-making for the charging action selection every 3 cycles, whereby the integration of battery aging states supports the reward function design as detailed in Methods, with the ultimate goal to extend the lifespan of solid-state batteries and attempt to eliminate the kneepoints.

To effectively leverage the hidden electrochemical information stored in the shape feature of battery voltage profiles, a method of treating them as 2-dimensional (2D) images is employed to combine with generalized image neural network (Fig. 2c), where the image includes current value, voltage shape, and capacity. To present the time-sequence information during cycling, the data of every 3-cycle is integrated into R, G, B channels of the shape image, respectively. Each data point here in the cycle has equal significance represented as pixels in the 2D image, which is more robust than the original 1D vector form as it is less affected by numerical values. With the augmentation of battery dataset in the future, more complex large models can also be employed to achieve generalization effects.

For the intelligence cycling module, a range of charging strategies is provided with different C-rates and voltage cutoffs (Fig. 2d). To avoid the additional complexity from optimized multi-stage CC-CV charging 27 and varying discharging current within each cycle 30, in our proof-of-concept demonstration here only the galvanostatic strategies within each cycle are adopted, although all these strategies are compatible with our methodology and can in principle be built into the platform in the future. C-rate (15~20C) and voltage cutoff (4.2~4.3V) are defined as parameters within a relatively small range of variation to exclude big change of specific capacity and related lifetime change directly caused by different charging strategies. A total of 18 available charging actions with a range of area capacity (0.309~0.438 mAh/cm2) can be combined from different C-rates and cutoffs, which are sorted for the intelligence cycling module. The AI agent then outputs the online selection of charging actions based on the real-time battery states and shape features, thereby dynamically achieving updated decisions of fast charging strategies between cycles. Through integrated control of solid-state batteries, closed-loop experiments are performed with acceptable timescales at the level of 15~20C-rate of charging speed. A single intelligent cycling experiment typically requires the occupancy of the AI channel for two to three weeks, during which these parameters of charging actions are fully utilized. Note that the area capacity can be further increased to 3 mAh/cm2 based on a different negative electrode configuration reported by us earlier 33, however, it will limit the C-rate of cycling within 5C, slow down the proof-of-concept demonstration here by around 5 times.

The solid-state batteries with intelligent cycling show significantly improved capacity retention and aging trajectory (Fig. 3). The batteries of both the intelligent cycling and the benchmark control with fixed CC cycling were tested multiple times for statistically significant comparison. The SOH range above 80% was selected for analyzing the longevity of batteries, where the advantages of intelligent cycling became increasingly evident. Above 90% SOH, there is no significant difference between intelligence and benchmark. As the SOH declined to 80%, the average total cycles under the intelligent cycling condition increases significantly, reaching 265% (1915 vs. 723) of the benchmark value (Fig. 3a), while the accumulated specific energy, based on the active material, achieves a 250% enhancement (Fig. 3b). A further segment analysis by every 5% SOH reveal that the average number of cycles within each segment consistently declined for the benchmark, while that of the intelligent cycling initially increased, with the highest capacity retention observed in the 90% to 85% SOH interval. This trend culminated in an over 550% increment in the cycle count from 90% to 80% SOH compared to the benchmark. (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b).

Figure 3c presents the cycling results of 7 benchmark batteries, whereby all exhibited the kneepoint feature in their capacity retention performance. The benchmark conditions were fixed within the regime of intelligent charging actions, where 18C-4.25V was selected as a representative midpoint. This allows a meaningful and quantifiable comparison with the intelligent cycling, which dynamically explores C-rates and voltage cutoffs both above and below this benchmark. Also, three of the benchmark cells were cycled at 20C-rate, and their performance was found to be comparable to those cycled at 18C-rate. This reinforces the representativeness and robustness of the chosen benchmark condition of 18C-rate and highlights that higher C-rates do not necessarily lead to inferior cycling performance in solid-state lithium metal batteries, which is consistent with our earlier findings 5.

The representative result of intelligent cycling is shown in Fig. 3d, where no kneepoint before 80% SOH was observed. Specifically, the charging actions dynamically adjust the C-rate and cutoff voltage, allowing the battery to oscillate between stable and transitional states (Fig. 3d, e). This behavior effectively delays or eliminates the emergence of kneepoints, which significantly extended the battery lifetime. Note that when monitoring the battery state during intelligent cycling, we find that different charging actions correspond to distinct changes in battery states, as reflected in statistical results (Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). The stable state is more frequently associated with higher C-rates, while the transitional state is primarily concentrated in the lower C-rate range.

To better understand the mechanisms underlying the intelligent cycling, the battery states were analyzed according to the corresponding selections of charging actions (Fig. 4a). With cycling, although the battery begins to enter the transitional state in the lower C-rate action region, the higher C-rate actions still maintain the stable state. Thereby when the intelligent cycling automatically jumps between high and low C-rates, the strategy seems to provide alternative pathways for the battery state evolution, where a transitional state can go back to the stable state. By dynamic navigation of actions, it can bypass irreversible degradation regimes and maintain the cycling stability of batteries, even under the well-known electrochemical stress of high C-rates. In contrast, the benchmark battery with fixed charging actions lacks such capability, quickly entering the sustained transitional state at an earlier cycle index, with the capacity kneepoint emerging accordingly (Fig. 4d). These results demonstrate that intelligent cycling significantly prolongs the stable operation phase. As cycling further progresses, the battery inevitably approaches a point where degradation becomes irreversible. Around 2000 cycles, the state perception output shifts to 1 across most action indices, indicating that the available charging actions to preserve the battery in a stable state are limited. This simultaneous onset of transitional states across large number of actions signals the transition of battery into an irreversible degradation. This behavior highlights the ultimate constraint of the electrochemical system, reflecting the capability limit of intelligent cycling to recover the battery to a stable state.

Shape images as the input for the neural network can be dimensionally reduced through principal component analysis (PCA). By integrating and reshaping the first three principal components (PC1, PC2, PC3) of all shape images, they largely capture the features such as capacity and voltage reduction with the cycling process (Supplementary Fig. 4). Specifically, PC1 reflects the global capacity fading trend (noted by horizontal shrinking of voltage plateaus), while PC2 and PC3 are linked to local fluctuations and distortions, likely representing internal resistance changes or interfacial instability. The distribution and motion trends of PC1-PC2 in the PCA space extracted from the voltage part of shape images reveal distinctions between intelligent cycling and the benchmark. The variability of charging actions in intelligent cycling inevitably introduces some confounding effects into the PCA results. Therefore, the PCA analysis should not be regarded as a direct indicator of state-of-health, but rather as a visualization tool to trace the evolution of battery state features. The PCA data points for intelligent cycling exhibit a divergent band pattern under charging actions, expanding over a larger area of PCA space (Fig. 4b). This suggests the intelligent cycling of dynamic strategy enables a broader and more flexible exploration of electrochemical states, allowing the battery to jump between states of little path dependence and hence access the principal component space that otherwise will be inaccessible in a normal cycling of fixed strategy, where unidirectional trajectory evolution in the principal component space shows a strong path dependence. Euclidean distances calculated between adjacent cycles in the PCA space quantify the state transitions induced by each action step composed of three consecutive cycles (Fig. 4c). For intelligent cycling, these distances reveal more frequent and larger shifts between consecutive steps, reflecting rapid and often reversible transitions between stable and transitional states, which effectively elongates the trajectory of the state evolution in the PCA space and slows down the degradation. In comparison, benchmark cycling exhibits narrow, unidirectional state trajectory (Fig. 4e) and minimal Euclidean displacement (Fig. 4f), corresponding to irreversible degradation and early emergence of knee points. The limited state variability under fixed charging actions restrict the ability to recover once degradation accelerates.

Regarding the interface reaction evolution shown in Fig. 2b, the cross-sections of batteries after the two different types of cycling were observed by SEM (Fig. 4g). The interface remained dense under intelligent cycling after 1700 cycles, whereas voids obviously present under the benchmark cycling condition after 1500 cycles. The evolution of electrochemical reactions inside the battery during cycling is often nonlinear. More specifically, the unique interface reaction pattern with a certain periodicity of reaction spots in Fig. 2b (ii) suggests the presence of long-range interactions between those spots. To simulate the effects of dynamic charging actions during intelligent cycling, we proposed a simple 2D grid model by assuming that the parameter determining the interaction field can fluctuate, corresponding to the perturbation introduced by varying charging actions (Methods). Simulations reveal that as this fluctuation ratio increases, the decomposition pattern can change from sparse degradation points with severe decomposition at each point to a more uniform and denser pattern with less severe degradation at each point (Supplementary Fig. 5). Additionally, we observed that the average degradation extent initially decreases and then increases as the fluctuation ratio grows. This behavior arises from a trade-off between the decreasing degradation extent at individual points and the increasing number of degradation points. These findings provide an intuitive picture to further discuss the effect of the varying charging actions, suggesting that although it can improve cycling longevity, excessive fluctuation may lead to diminishing rewards.

This prediction is supported by our experiment, where the impact of increasing number of charging actions was evaluated through manually pre-programmed battery testing procedures (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 6). Comparing those tests with fewer actions of 2 or 4 (Supplementary Fig. 6a–c) and with more actions of 6 (Supplementary Fig. 6d, e) with the action switch of every 50 cycles, it shows that increasing the number of actions helps the retention before the effect of action number converges at 6 actions. All the 18 charging actions were executed in the random action test (Supplementary Fig. 6h) and were updated every 3 cycles, matching the interval and actions used in intelligent cycling. The lower capacity retention in the random action test than the intelligent one and the 6-actions one suggest the importance of intelligent cycling when more actions (e.g. 18) are included, without the need to test and program the optimum number of actions and the frequency to switch them. Action number dependence (Fig. 4h) offers insight into the underlying mechanisms of increasing charging complexity. By comparing cycling performance up to 1500 cycles, a correlation emerges between the number of available charging actions and battery longevity. Varying both C-rate and cutoff can work, however, the action number is not linearly proportional to the performance improvement, tending to saturate beyond a certain point. Notably, under the same available action number, test with randomly varied charging actions exhibits no knee point, but the capacity decay is significantly faster than the average results achieved with the intelligent cycling. The 6 cutoff group shows slightly higher capacity retention at 1500 cycles compared to intelligent cycling. This outcome likely reflects the effect of diminishing rewards when increasing the number of available charging actions beyond a certain level. As also illustrated in the 2D grid model (Supplementary Fig. 5), a moderate level of fluctuation may strike the balance between the extent and distribution of local degradations, leading to temporarily favorable outcomes. The 6-cutoff group may happen to lie near such a marginal optimum. However, given the abrupt nature of capacity knee points, short-term advantages in capacity retention don't necessarily imply improved long-term performance. Intelligent cycling is thus designed to dynamically adapt to evolving battery states, aiming to delay the onset of irreversible degradation automatically.

In summary, this work opens a promising direction of real-time AI for battery management system, by integrating machine intelligence with real-time charging strategies to enhance the battery longevity and safety, as demonstrated with solid-state lithium metal batteries. By enabling real-time perception and regulation of battery states, the proposed intelligent cycling approach achieves significant improvements in cycle life and accumulated specific energy at high current density, minimizing dendrite growth related interface reaction issues. Our approach also fully utilizes the information stored in the voltage and current profiles, minimizing the reliance on physical sensors and thus reducing the device-level cost. The method is also compatible with advanced fast charging strategies, such as multi-stage CC-CV protocols, and varying operational external pressure or environmental temperature, etc., highlighting its adaptability to diverse application scenarios. Moreover, the realization of state perception enables the proactive prediction and mitigation of adverse battery states. Moving forward, the integration of this framework is expected to be broadly adaptable to commercial battery systems, and its compatibility with edge computing devices 34 will present opportunities for even smarter, decentralized battery management systems, ensuring enhanced reliability and safety in next-generation energy storage solutions.

---

## Methods

Real-time connection platform
A custom real-time connection platform was developed to enable closed-loop cycling control between the AI module and the battery testing station. Recently developed modular architecture can enable rapid development of efficient hardware designs for various applications 35. The platform integrates a Python-based control on a computer workstation with the battery testing hardware (Solartron XM MTS) for real-time data exchange and parameter updates. Notably, this implementation does not rely on proprietary software modifications to the hardware. The control system was implemented using Component Object Model (COM) automation Application Programming Interface (API), which expose programmable interfaces for accessing and managing hardware operations, including experiment execution, instrument status monitoring, and data retrieval. An established Python environment running was used to interact with these COM interfaces, enabling direct control from the workstation. Physically, the workstation is connected to the Solartron system through a standard Registered Jack 45 (RJ-45) Ethernet interface over Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP). The instrument is visible on the local network and can be accessed through its assigned IP address. The latency introduced by the closed loop is negligible relative to the cycling timescale. Reliability is also ensured by leveraging the same standard interface used in routine experiments, with no observable disruption or delay during long-term operation. For broader applicability, commercial vendors generally confirmed that modern programmable battery testers support external integration via open interfaces. Therefore, the proposed platform is broadly transferable across different hardware systems.

State perception module
The relevant dataset includes 28 all-solid-state batteries with the knee point feature with the C-rate ranging from 1C to 25C. Despite the diversity in data sources, all solid-state cells share the same electrochemical configuration that NMC811 positive electrodes paired with lithium metal negative electrodes. These electrolyte differences among the cells introduce measurable variations in degradation behavior, which can evaluate the neural network’s generalization performance across different degradation pathways. Importantly, the model was not trained to target any specific failure mechanism, allowing it to capture broader degradation dynamics without overfitting to a particular pathway.

The batteries used in subsequent intelligence and benchmark tests were excluded from the training and validation of the state perception model, there by preserving the generality and independence of this dataset. We previously found that treating voltage curves during battery cycling as 2D images and then encoding them can enable the shape feature vectors to successfully uncover hidden battery information for machine learning-based predictions of commercial Li-ion batteries 36,37. Here, we fully retain both current and voltage information, and more importantly make the 2D image of each cycle equivalently represent each data point by pixels, rather than the previous method of using less robust numerical values in the 1D shape feature vector. According to the natural RGB channels of images, the data of every 3-cycle is integrated into one shape image for time-sequence information during cycling.

State perception module is based on residual network 50 (ResNet50) 38, which is fed with the above shape images as the input. A total of 83,422 such samples were used for training. The overall dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets at a 16:6:6 ratio, corresponding approximately to 60%, 20%, and 20% of the full 28 batteries. The detailed configurations of the batteries were masked during dataset preparation. Each battery’s data was included exclusively in one subset to prevent data leakage and ensure generalization to unseen batteries.

The overall prediction accuracies for validation and test reach 89% and 86%, respectively. The confusion matrix provides specific insight into the performance evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 7), with detailed metrics summarized in Supplementary Table 1. Low precision means a true battery state is more likely to be predicted erroneously than missed, while low recall implies that the true battery state is more likely to be missed than falsely predicted. Both stable and decay states consistently indicate high precision and high recall, ensuring reliable identification. For the transitional state, missing its truth will risk missing the warnings of rapid capacity decay caused by an approaching knee point, undermining the battery cycling stability and the protection by the intelligent cycling. Therefore, the overall prediction performance prioritizes high recall across all states. By the recall-focused F2-score metric, the analysis confirms that the online prediction is robust and reliable across different battery states.

Intelligent cycling framework
To optimize the adaptive fast charging strategies across cycles, we employed the reinforcement learning (RL) approach using a Deep Q-Network (DQN), as noted by long-timescale research 39. The model, implemented via Stable-Baselines3 40, was specifically tailored here for analyzing all-solid-state batteries. Here the intelligent cycling framework operated in a closed loop comprising the experimental environment, the state perception module, and the AI agent (Supplementary Fig. 8) 41. Every 3-cycle data was processed into shape image that served as the input to state perception module and the variable in observation space for the AI agent. Charging strategies are constituted of a range of action space, allowing the AI agent to utilize charging actions. As the outputs of the perception module represent the current battery states, the reward function is comprehensively designed by integrating three components: the current battery state, the selected action with C-rate and cutoff, and the coincided degree of shape feature across three consecutive cycles. For state rewards, when the perception module outputs a stable state, the state reward component is +1, activating the action-based rewards for the C-rate and cutoff. Within this framework, the reward favors high C-rate and cutoff values and penalizes lower values within a reward value of −0.5 to +0.5. When the battery state becomes transitional, the state reward is −1, and the state reward drops to −5 for the decay state. For the shape feature reward, a threshold is set to mitigate the influence of drastic capacity changes. Significant deviations in capacity curves across 3 cycles incurred penalties, while well-coincided shape features were rewarded, with values ranging from −0.4 to +0.4. Finally, the intelligent cycling framework selected optimal charging actions within the predefined range. This design balances the exploration of high-performance charging strategies while maintaining stability and avoiding rapid degradation. Multiple-experiment results of intelligent cycling and benchmark batteries are provided in Supplementary Figs. 9–14 and Supplementary Note 1.

Materials
The precursor of Li5.5PS4.5Cl1.5 (LPSCl) solid electrolyte was synthesized via planetary ball milling of Li2S (99.9%, Alfa Aesar), P2S5 (99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and LiCl (99%, Alfa Aesar) in a stoichiometric ratio. The starting materials were ball milled under argon atmosphere in 80 mL ZrO2 jars for 16 h at 460 rpm in a planetary ball mill PM200 (Retsch GmbH, Germany). Eighteen 10-mm Y-ZrO2 beads were paired with 2 g starting materials in total. The ball milling program was set to be a cyclic process of 10 min milling and 2 min resting. The resulting precursor was then sintered in a quartz tube at 550 °C for 1 h in an argon gas flow. The sintered product was ground with a mortar and pestle for subsequent applications. The Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS) solid electrolyte was a commercial product from MSE Supplies.

Battery assembly
We designed the positive electrode loading and N/P ratio of all-solid-state batteries with multi-layer electrolyte as separator, graphite covered lithium metal as negative electrode, and NMC as positive electrode for fast charging experiments by modifying our previous battery configuration 5. The positive electrode for the all-solid-state batteries was fabricated into a homogeneous dry film by mixing 70 wt% LiNi0.82Mn0.07Co0.11O2 (MSE Supplies), 30 wt% as-prepared LPSCl and 3 wt% extra PTFE powders and repetitive calendaring with stainless steel plate and stick. The positive electrode film was punched into 1/4” disks for battery assembly. The negative electrode was a graphite-protected lithium metal foil. A uniform graphite film was made by mixing natural graphite (MSE Supplies) and 5 wt% PTFE powders. The graphite film was punched into a 5/16” disk and carefully attached to a 1/4” thin lithium metal foil. During battery assembly, the negative electrode film, 30 mg of LPSCl, 110 mg of LGPS, 30 mg of LPSCl and the positive electrode film were stacked in sequence in a PTFE casing under an argon atmosphere. A formation pressure of 387 MPa was exerted and maintained for 1 min to fulfill sufficient contact and a stacking pressure of around 150 MPa was kept during battery cycling. Positive electrode loading is correlated with battery aging trajectory at fixed layer thickness of graphite and lithium layers (Supplementary Fig. 15). As the loading increases and N/P ratio decreases in this battery system, knee point occurs earlier and eventually disappears with severe capacity decay at the beginning of cycling. Accordingly, we selected the positive electrode loading of 2.58 mg/cm2 and fixed the graphite film weight as 2 mg and lithium metal foil weight as 0.8 mg, which makes the knee point occurs stably in a cycling index range that is meaningful to the current project. Note that further reducing the positive electrode loading below 2.58 mg/cm2 and increasing the N/P ratio will make the battery too stable and severely delay the occurrence of the knee point, impeding a rapid development for this proof-of-concept test and demo. The battery measurements were conducted on Arbin BT2000 and Solartron XM MTS respectively for benchmark and intelligence tests, in 55 °C environment chambers. It is worth noting that the positive electrode loading can be increased above 15 mg/cm2, and the operational pressure can be reduced below 25 MPa in a pouch cell, although the cycling C-rate must be reduced to 5C 33. Although the reduced C-rate will slow down the proof-of-concept test by 5 times, the more practical pouch cell is also compatible with our AI platform of more complicated charging procedures in the future.

Scanning electron microscopy & energy-dispersive spectroscopy
Solid-state batteries were transferred to an argon-filled glovebox after cycling to various stages and disassembled for characterization. Samples for morphological and elemental measurements were prepared by blade cutting multilayer pellets, exposing flat cross sections. Samples were then sealed in aluminum bags under argon atmosphere and sent to the electron microscope. The entire sampling process was conducted at a temperature of 25 ± 0.5 °C. Cross-sectional images of cycled batteries were captured under the secondary electron mode of ZEISS Gemini SEM 560. An acceleration voltage of 5.00 kV, an aperture of 20.00 μm, and a working distance ~6 mm were used. For elemental mapping of sulfur, phosphorus, oxygen, and others in the cross sections, the backscattered electron mode of the instrument was employed with an acceleration voltage of 15.00 kV, an aperture of 60.00 μm, and a working distance of around 10 mm. Cross-sectional images emphasizing atomic-number differences were captured with such settings as well. All samples were sealed and transferred while maintaining an argon atmosphere to minimize air exposure.

Grid simulation
A 2D grid model is developed to simulate the influence of varying charging actions on the growth of decomposition spots as observed in SEM. Although the exact origin of the long-range interactions among these spots still remains unidentified, they are most likely the result of plastic strain field caused by local decompositions and the interaction of the field with ion conductions. We hypothesize that these fields govern the growth rate of existing decomposition points and the formation of additional ones. The interaction field generated by a decomposition point suppresses decomposition near its core, potentially due to current redistribution or strain field effects. At moderate distances, the field promotes decomposition, which could arise from increased current shunted from the core. Each point on a 2D grid (x, y) represents the extent of decomposition, u(x, y). A point is considered undecomposed if u(x, y) = 0, and decomposed otherwise, with the value of u(x, y) > 0 indicating the extent of decomposition at that point. The decomposition extent is irreversible, meaning that u(x, y) can only increase over time. Decomposition at each point is influenced by an interaction field generated by other decomposed points. The interaction field at a point (x, y) due to a decomposed point i with decomposition extent ui is assumed as: fi(u, r) = ui(r−3 − r−4), where r is the distance from point i to (x, y), computed as: r = sqrt((x − xi)2 + (y − yi)2). The decay proportional to r−3 is analogous to the solution of Laplace’s equation under a no-flux boundary condition for a spherical geometry. The parameter fluctuates as a(t) = a0(1 + rf cos t) where rf is called the fluctuation ratio. The total field at each point (x, y) combines the contributions from the interaction fields of all decomposed points and a base field B: F(x, y) = sum(fi(ui, r)) + B. At a point with existing decomposition (u(x, y) > 0), the decomposition grows as du(x, y)/dt = max(0, λgrowth * F(x, y)) where λgrowth is a constant controlling the growth rate. At an undecomposed point (u(x, y) = 0), the probability of forming a new decomposition center (u(x, y) is set to u0) in each time step dt is given by: P = λnew * F(x, y) * dt, where λnew is a constant determining the likelihood of nucleation.

This work presents a closed-loop battery testing platform incorporating AI for real-time adaptive cycling. The authors propose

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Battery health often evolves from an initial regime of slow capacity decay to a fast decay regime, due to catastrophic electrochemical reactions to cause the battery failure. The signals of such failure, however, often emerge much earlier during cycling, an early detection of which may help prevent the failure through real-time adjustment of cycling procedures. Here we demonstrate the integration of machine learning module directly into electrochemical battery test stations to constantly detect the signals from battery current and voltage profiles, followed by reinforcement learning–based real-time adjustment of cycling procedures for greatly elongated battery lifetime. We use solid-state lithium metal batteries to demonstrate this proof-of-concept implementation of built-in intelligence for future battery management systems, leveraging their high current density and fast cycling to generate abundant data and greatly shorten the development feedback loop. This intelligent approach improves battery lifetime by 265% and accumulative specific energy based on active material by 250% at 80% state of health, which is achieved through an effective control of detrimental interface reactions. This work showcases a pathway toward real-time artificial intelligence control of batteries for longevity and safety beyond human expertise.

---

## Introduction

The Li-ion battery is one of the most powerful technologies in our era for decarbonization and combating climate change 1–4. The longevity and safety concerns, however, constantly challenge its applications since the birth of the technology. One typical failure mode in Li-ion battery is the lithium dendrite induced short circuits or side reactions. The development of solid-state batteries shows that Li dendrite penetration may be prevented through hierarchical structure and interface designs of the negative electrode and electrolyte layers 5–8. However, Li dendrite can still cause various problems in solid-state batteries through its high reactivity with electrolyte and negative electrode materials 9–13, where fast capacity decay upon cycling can often be observed. For example, in Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2a, these solid-state batteries tested in our lab used relatively low negative to positive electrode capacity ratios (N/P ratio), which is preferred for practical batteries but is also a factor that can often boost Li dendrite growth or interface reaction, and hence battery failure. The capacity retention of these batteries is nonlinear, often with a “kneepoint” 14–16, beyond which rapid decline in capacity occurs. The origin of the kneepoint is complicated and lacks unified explanations 17,18. In Li-ion battery, it can often be caused by Li dendrite penetration induced internal short circuit, while in our solid-state batteries it is more likely related to the Li dendrite growth induced interface reactions. When the kneepoint appears in the battery cycling, both state of health (SOH) and remaining useful life (RUL) will drop quickly. SOH and RUL are two performance metrics widely used in the battery industry to describe the status of batteries. Previous modeling and artificial intelligence (AI) based methods also focused on the two metrics in their predictions 19–23. Nevertheless, the emergence of the kneepoint always challenges the prediction due to the dramatic change of capacity decay rate across the point 14,24.

For a given battery configuration, it was noticed that charging strategy can influence the lifetime 25,26. Derived from the primitive constant current (CC) and constant voltage (CV), the various fast charging strategies nowadays are mainly categorized into multi-stage CC-CV or pulse current based on charging waveform 27,28 and optimization control based on battery models 29,30. However, online modulation of charging strategies with battery cycling based on the real-time status of a running battery has not been implemented, as it requires real-time diagnosis of batteries and the decision-making capability of the program. In most previous cases, a charging strategy was firstly optimized and then the fixed strategy was executed to every cycle throughout the cycling test.

In this work, we develop a platform, as depicted in Fig. 1a, where the machine learning intelligence, consisting of two key modules of state perception and intelligent cycling, is connected with a running battery through the battery test station. The tester operates as both the experimental instrument and the physical main body for real-time integration of the AI agent running on the workstation. The platform can thus monitor the current battery state and then based on the detected data in previous N cycles decide how to change the battery cycling procedures for any following N cycles, where N is chosen to be 3 and the cycling procedures include various C-rates (1C = 150 mA/g) and voltage cutoffs in this particular work. As shown in the detailed workflow (Fig. 1b), the AI workstation directly communicates with the tester hardware via physical connection of COM APIs over TCP/IP. Every 3-cycle data is employed to evaluate the battery state and adaptively control the charging strategy. This implementation supports real-time closed-loop control without relying on proprietary vendor software.

As a proof-of-concept demonstration, we utilize the fast charging and discharging capability of our solid-state batteries to 20C-rate at low positive electrode loading 5, to greatly accelerate the data generation and reduce the feedback time in the proof-of-concept development. This enabled rapid lifetime cycling and efficient model iteration. While commercial Li-ion batteries offer better reproducibility, their limited rate capability would substantially prolong the experimental timeline, especially under AI-extended lifetimes. However, implementing our approach to commercial Li-ion battery and BMS system will be an obvious next step through the collaboration with the battery industry. Nonetheless, our strategy in principle could also be adapted to conventional Li-ion batteries or systems.

---

## Results

Our results highlight the built-in intelligence for fast charging capability of solid-state lithium metal batteries, where both longevity and SOH stability of batteries are greatly improved. In comparison with the control batteries with conventional fixed strategies, our real-time AI for battery charging strategy significantly postponed or even prevented the occurrence of the kneepoint before the industrial standard of 80% SOH. It is worth noting that neither the authors, the research field as far as we know, nor our AI platform has any a priori knowledge of a clear microscopic failure mechanism related to the kneepoint of these batteries. Interestingly, however, our experimental characterization and computational modeling later show that AI did identify an optimal strategy within our framework to modulate the evolution of the most relevant interface reaction, with the mechanism being discussed. This suggests the potential of such AI platform to help achieve fundamental understandings in battery electrochemistry as well.

More specifically, the state perception module detects battery states evolution with cycling in three different states of stable, transitional, and decay ones (Fig. 2a). While 0.8 SOH is commonly used in industrial settings as the end-of-life (EOL) threshold, the definition of state segmentation is to isolate and examine the rapid degradation behavior around the knee point. The transitional state represents a temporary yet critical period where internal failures and side reactions accelerate and have not yet stabilized. That means a battery in the transitional state, especially in an early stage of the state, can possibly return to the stable state through intelligent cycling (e.g., Fig. 2d, e). Only after the fast degradation phase does the battery enter the final decay state, characterized by a slower rate of capacity loss at very low capacities. The transitional state contains the kneepoint, with the two boundaries decided by first and second derivatives in a capacity retention profile. The left boundary of the transitional state is defined as when the acceleration, or second derivative, becomes continuously negative, and the right boundary is when velocity, or the first derivative, reaches its minimum negative value. The state definition here is supported by our experimental characterization and reflects the evolution of dominant electrochemical reactions in the batteries.

These solid-state batteries follow a configuration of NMC811 as positive electrode, multilayer electrolytes as separator, and Li/Graphite as negative electrode, i.e., Li/Graphite|LPSCl|LGPS|LPSCl|NMC811, where NMC811 represents LiNi0.82Mn0.07Co0.11O2, LPSCl represents Li5.5PS4.5Cl1.5 and LGPS represents Li10GeP2S12. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) cross-section images of the batteries at different cycling stages in Fig. 2b show the evolution of reactions at the LGPS|LPSCl interface. In the stable state, the interface remains overall intact, with only isolated dark spots occasionally observed, suggesting that the local area is with low Z number in chemical elements based on the contrast mechanism of the backscattered electron microscopy. As the battery progresses into the transitional state with cycling, more black points stay close to each other at the interface and eventually connect into a black line region in the decay state. Deep into the decay state, the interface region becomes thicker with voids but less dark 31,32. Energy dispersive X-Ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping further shows that the dark regions is rich in O and Ge, deficient in P and S (Supplementary Fig. 2), indicating the evolution is dominated by interface reactions between Li metal dendrite and LGPS electrolyte, with Li-Ge-rich local decomposition products initially generated at the transitional state and more elements of S and Cl later enter the reaction region deep into the decay state. Note although Li cannot be directly detected by EDS, it can react with oxygen thus trap them locally to mark the location of Li.

A historical dataset in the research group of such Li||NMC811 solid-state batteries with the knee point feature in the capacity retention test (Supplementary Fig. 1) was further used to train the neural network in order to predict the state of a running battery from the voltage and current data (Methods). Notably, this dataset is very scalable as it is generated by diverse solid-state batteries by various group members for different projects previously, rather than coming from a dedicated collection for this particular project. That said, the consistent positive electrode/negative electrode configuration ensures a focused evaluation of the ability of our model to generalize across different degradation patterns induced by electrolyte variations. To construct the training samples, each battery is not treated as the data unit; instead, the model ingests abundant 3-cycle segmental data from the entire cycling of each cell as the data unit.

The state perception module can read the running battery on the voltage and current data of every 3 cycles. Since the geometrical shape details in voltage profiles as an ensemble reflect the collective behavior of the internal electrochemical reactions, the state perception module, equivalently speaking, monitor these reactions in situ for a working battery, providing sufficient nonlinearity and complexity for the input layer of deep neural network (DNN) models. The real-time state information of the past 3 cycles each time is then fed into the intelligent cycling module to evaluate how to change the charging strategies for the next 3 cycles. We employ reinforcement learning (RL) to provide dynamic decision-making for the charging action selection every 3 cycles, whereby the integration of battery aging states supports the reward function design as detailed in Methods, with the ultimate goal to extend the lifespan of solid-state batteries and attempt to eliminate the kneepoints.

To effectively leverage the hidden electrochemical information stored in the shape feature of battery voltage profiles, a method of treating them as 2-dimensional (2D) images is employed to combine with generalized image neural network (Fig. 2c), where the image includes current value, voltage shape, and capacity. To present the time-sequence information during cycling, the data of every 3-cycle is integrated into R, G, B channels of the shape image, respectively. Each data point here in the cycle has equal significance represented as pixels in the 2D image, which is more robust than the original 1D vector form as it is less affected by numerical values. With the augmentation of battery dataset in the future, more complex large models can also be employed to achieve generalization effects.

For the intelligence cycling module, a range of charging strategies is provided with different C-rates and voltage cutoffs (Fig. 2d). To avoid the additional complexity from optimized multi-stage CC-CV charging 27 and varying discharging current within each cycle 30, in our proof-of-concept demonstration here only the galvanostatic strategies within each cycle are adopted, although all these strategies are compatible with our methodology and can in principle be built into the platform in the future. C-rate (15~20C) and voltage cutoff (4.2~4.3V) are defined as parameters within a relatively small range of variation to exclude big change of specific capacity and related lifetime change directly caused by different charging strategies. A total of 18 available charging actions with a range of area capacity (0.309~0.438 mAh/cm2) can be combined from different C-rates and cutoffs, which are sorted for the intelligence cycling module. The AI agent then outputs the online selection of charging actions based on the real-time battery states and shape features, thereby dynamically achieving updated decisions of fast charging strategies between cycles. Through integrated control of solid-state batteries, closed-loop experiments are performed with acceptable timescales at the level of 15~20C-rate of charging speed. A single intelligent cycling experiment typically requires the occupancy of the AI channel for two to three weeks, during which these parameters of charging actions are fully utilized. Note that the area capacity can be further increased to 3 mAh/cm2 based on a different negative electrode configuration reported by us earlier 33, however, it will limit the C-rate of cycling within 5C, slow down the proof-of-concept demonstration here by around 5 times.

The solid-state batteries with intelligent cycling show significantly improved capacity retention and aging trajectory (Fig. 3). The batteries of both the intelligent cycling and the benchmark control with fixed CC cycling were tested multiple times for statistically significant comparison. The SOH range above 80% was selected for analyzing the longevity of batteries, where the advantages of intelligent cycling became increasingly evident. Above 90% SOH, there is no significant difference between intelligence and benchmark. As the SOH declined to 80%, the average total cycles under the intelligent cycling condition increases significantly, reaching 265% (1915 vs. 723) of the benchmark value (Fig. 3a), while the accumulated specific energy, based on the active material, achieves a 250% enhancement (Fig. 3b). A further segment analysis by every 5% SOH reveal that the average number of cycles within each segment consistently declined for the benchmark, while that of the intelligent cycling initially increased, with the highest capacity retention observed in the 90% to 85% SOH interval. This trend culminated in an over 550% increment in the cycle count from 90% to 80% SOH compared to the benchmark. (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b).

Figure 3c presents the cycling results of 7 benchmark batteries, whereby all exhibited the kneepoint feature in their capacity retention performance. The benchmark conditions were fixed within the regime of intelligent charging actions, where 18C-4.25V was selected as a representative midpoint. This allows a meaningful and quantifiable comparison with the intelligent cycling, which dynamically explores C-rates and voltage cutoffs both above and below this benchmark. Also, three of the benchmark cells were cycled at 20C-rate, and their performance was found to be comparable to those cycled at 18C-rate. This reinforces the representativeness and robustness of the chosen benchmark condition of 18C-rate and highlights that higher C-rates do not necessarily lead to inferior cycling performance in solid-state lithium metal batteries, which is consistent with our earlier findings 5.

The representative result of intelligent cycling is shown in Fig. 3d, where no kneepoint before 80% SOH was observed. Specifically, the charging actions dynamically adjust the C-rate and cutoff voltage, allowing the battery to oscillate between stable and transitional states (Fig. 3d, e). This behavior effectively delays or eliminates the emergence of kneepoints, which significantly extended the battery lifetime. Note that when monitoring the battery state during intelligent cycling, we find that different charging actions correspond to distinct changes in battery states, as reflected in statistical results (Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). The stable state is more frequently associated with higher C-rates, while the transitional state is primarily concentrated in the lower C-rate range.

To better understand the mechanisms underlying the intelligent cycling, the battery states were analyzed according to the corresponding selections of charging actions (Fig. 4a). With cycling, although the battery begins to enter the transitional state in the lower C-rate action region, the higher C-rate actions still maintain the stable state. Thereby when the intelligent cycling automatically jumps between high and low C-rates, the strategy seems to provide alternative pathways for the battery state evolution, where a transitional state can go back to the stable state. By dynamic navigation of actions, it can bypass irreversible degradation regimes and maintain the cycling stability of batteries, even under the well-known electrochemical stress of high C-rates. In contrast, the benchmark battery with fixed charging actions lacks such capability, quickly entering the sustained transitional state at an earlier cycle index, with the capacity kneepoint emerging accordingly (Fig. 4d). These results demonstrate that intelligent cycling significantly prolongs the stable operation phase. As cycling further progresses, the battery inevitably approaches a point where degradation becomes irreversible. Around 2000 cycles, the state perception output shifts to 1 across most action indices, indicating that the available charging actions to preserve the battery in a stable state are limited. This simultaneous onset of transitional states across large number of actions signals the transition of battery into an irreversible degradation. This behavior highlights the ultimate constraint of the electrochemical system, reflecting the capability limit of intelligent cycling to recover the battery to a stable state.

Shape images as the input for the neural network can be dimensionally reduced through principal component analysis (PCA). By integrating and reshaping the first three principal components (PC1, PC2, PC3) of all shape images, they largely capture the features such as capacity and voltage reduction with the cycling process (Supplementary Fig. 4). Specifically, PC1 reflects the global capacity fading trend (noted by horizontal shrinking of voltage plateaus), while PC2 and PC3 are linked to local fluctuations and distortions, likely representing internal resistance changes or interfacial instability. The distribution and motion trends of PC1-PC2 in the PCA space extracted from the voltage part of shape images reveal distinctions between intelligent cycling and the benchmark. The variability of charging actions in intelligent cycling inevitably introduces some confounding effects into the PCA results. Therefore, the PCA analysis should not be regarded as a direct indicator of state-of-health, but rather as a visualization tool to trace the evolution of battery state features. The PCA data points for intelligent cycling exhibit a divergent band pattern under charging actions, expanding over a larger area of PCA space (Fig. 4b). This suggests the intelligent cycling of dynamic strategy enables a broader and more flexible exploration of electrochemical states, allowing the battery to jump between states of little path dependence and hence access the principal component space that otherwise will be inaccessible in a normal cycling of fixed strategy, where unidirectional trajectory evolution in the principal component space shows a strong path dependence. Euclidean distances calculated between adjacent cycles in the PCA space quantify the state transitions induced by each action step composed of three consecutive cycles (Fig. 4c). For intelligent cycling, these distances reveal more frequent and larger shifts between consecutive steps, reflecting rapid and often reversible transitions between stable and transitional states, which effectively elongates the trajectory of the state evolution in the PCA space and slows down the degradation. In comparison, benchmark cycling exhibits narrow, unidirectional state trajectory (Fig. 4e) and minimal Euclidean displacement (Fig. 4f), corresponding to irreversible degradation and early emergence of knee points. The limited state variability under fixed charging actions restrict the ability to recover once degradation accelerates.

Regarding the interface reaction evolution shown in Fig. 2b, the cross-sections of batteries after the two different types of cycling were observed by SEM (Fig. 4g). The interface remained dense under intelligent cycling after 1700 cycles, whereas voids obviously present under the benchmark cycling condition after 1500 cycles. The evolution of electrochemical reactions inside the battery during cycling is often nonlinear. More specifically, the unique interface reaction pattern with a certain periodicity of reaction spots in Fig. 2b (ii) suggests the presence of long-range interactions between those spots. To simulate the effects of dynamic charging actions during intelligent cycling, we proposed a simple 2D grid model by assuming that the parameter determining the interaction field can fluctuate, corresponding to the perturbation introduced by varying charging actions (Methods). Simulations reveal that as this fluctuation ratio increases, the decomposition pattern can change from sparse degradation points with severe decomposition at each point to a more uniform and denser pattern with less severe degradation at each point (Supplementary Fig. 5). Additionally, we observed that the average degradation extent initially decreases and then increases as the fluctuation ratio grows. This behavior arises from a trade-off between the decreasing degradation extent at individual points and the increasing number of degradation points. These findings provide an intuitive picture to further discuss the effect of the varying charging actions, suggesting that although it can improve cycling longevity, excessive fluctuation may lead to diminishing rewards.

This prediction is supported by our experiment, where the impact of increasing number of charging actions was evaluated through manually pre-programmed battery testing procedures (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 6). Comparing those tests with fewer actions of 2 or 4 (Supplementary Fig. 6a–c) and with more actions of 6 (Supplementary Fig. 6d, e) with the action switch of every 50 cycles, it shows that increasing the number of actions helps the retention before the effect of action number converges at 6 actions. All the 18 charging actions were executed in the random action test (Supplementary Fig. 6h) and were updated every 3 cycles, matching the interval and actions used in intelligent cycling. The lower capacity retention in the random action test than the intelligent one and the 6-actions one suggest the importance of intelligent cycling when more actions (e.g. 18) are included, without the need to test and program the optimum number of actions and the frequency to switch them. Action number dependence (Fig. 4h) offers insight into the underlying mechanisms of increasing charging complexity. By comparing cycling performance up to 1500 cycles, a correlation emerges between the number of available charging actions and battery longevity. Varying both C-rate and cutoff can work, however, the action number is not linearly proportional to the performance improvement, tending to saturate beyond a certain point. Notably, under the same available action number, test with randomly varied charging actions exhibits no knee point, but the capacity decay is significantly faster than the average results achieved with the intelligent cycling. The 6 cutoff group shows slightly higher capacity retention at 1500 cycles compared to intelligent cycling. This outcome likely reflects the effect of diminishing rewards when increasing the number of available charging actions beyond a certain level. As also illustrated in the 2D grid model (Supplementary Fig. 5), a moderate level of fluctuation may strike the balance between the extent and distribution of local degradations, leading to temporarily favorable outcomes. The 6-cutoff group may happen to lie near such a marginal optimum. However, given the abrupt nature of capacity knee points, short-term advantages in capacity retention don't necessarily imply improved long-term performance. Intelligent cycling is thus designed to dynamically adapt to evolving battery states, aiming to delay the onset of irreversible degradation automatically.

In summary, this work opens a promising direction of real-time AI for battery management system, by integrating machine intelligence with real-time charging strategies to enhance the battery longevity and safety, as demonstrated with solid-state lithium metal batteries. By enabling real-time perception and regulation of battery states, the proposed intelligent cycling approach achieves significant improvements in cycle life and accumulated specific energy at high current density, minimizing dendrite growth related interface reaction issues. Our approach also fully utilizes the information stored in the voltage and current profiles, minimizing the reliance on physical sensors and thus reducing the device-level cost. The method is also compatible with advanced fast charging strategies, such as multi-stage CC-CV protocols, and varying operational external pressure or environmental temperature, etc., highlighting its adaptability to diverse application scenarios. Moreover, the realization of state perception enables the proactive prediction and mitigation of adverse battery states. Moving forward, the integration of this framework is expected to be broadly adaptable to commercial battery systems, and its compatibility with edge computing devices 34 will present opportunities for even smarter, decentralized battery management systems, ensuring enhanced reliability and safety in next-generation energy storage solutions.
